groups.title: The DOM
groups.question: You are showing a user's comment on the page and animating a list as it grows, and the page feels janky. Explain how you change the page with the DOM safely and efficiently.

followUps.Selecting and changing nodes: Why is textContent safer than innerHTML for showing a user's comment?
followUps.Reflow and repaint cost: Why does reading an element's height right after changing its style slow things down?

evidence.text: You find elements with methods like querySelector and change them through their properties.
textContent treats the value as plain text, so any HTML in it is shown, not run.
innerHTML with user data can inject markup or scripts into the page.

notEnough: Only saying innerHTML is bad without explaining what can happen.

evidence.text: Changing styles can force the browser to recalculate layout and repaint.
Reading a layout value right after a change forces that recalculation to happen immediately.
Grouping all reads and then all writes avoids repeated recalculations.

notEnough: Only saying DOM changes are slow.

groups.title: Events
groups.question: You have a table with hundreds of rows, each with a delete button, and rows get added over time. You also want a smooth-scrolling page and separate widgets that react to each other. Explain how you would handle events.

followUps.Bubbling and delegation: Why can one listener on the table handle clicks for rows added later?
followUps.Passive listeners and custom events: What does marking a scroll listener passive change?

evidence.text: Most events travel up from the clicked element through its parents.
A single listener on a parent can check which child was clicked.
This also works for elements added after the listener was set up.

notEnough: Only saying events bubble without explaining delegation.

evidence.text: A passive listener promises not to cancel scrolling, so the browser can scroll without waiting for your code.
Custom events let one part of the page announce something that others can listen for.
That way parts of the page communicate without holding direct references to each other.

notEnough: Only saying passive listeners are faster.

groups.title: Storage
groups.question: Your app stores the user's login token, a draft message and a large list of offline products in the browser. Explain where each should live and why.

followUps.localStorage, sessionStorage and cookies: Why is localStorage a bad place for a login token?
followUps.IndexedDB and caching: When would you choose IndexedDB over localStorage?

evidence.text: localStorage can be read by any script running on the page, so injected scripts can steal what is there.
Web Storage is synchronous and stores only strings.
Cookies marked HttpOnly cannot be read by JavaScript and are sent with each request.

notEnough: Only saying localStorage is not secure without saying why.

misconceptions.text: Says sessionStorage is safe for secrets because it is cleared when the tab closes.

evidence.text: IndexedDB stores large amounts of structured data.
It is asynchronous, so it does not freeze the page while reading or writing.
The Cache API stores network responses so pages can work offline.

notEnough: Only saying IndexedDB is a database in the browser.

groups.title: Observation and Navigation
groups.question: You want images to load only when they scroll into view, a chart to resize with its container, and tabs that change the URL without reloading. Explain how browser APIs help with each.

followUps.Intersection and Resize observers: Why is an IntersectionObserver better than checking positions in a scroll handler?
followUps.History API: How can a single-page app change the URL without a page reload, and what happens on the back button?

evidence.text: Observers tell you when an element becomes visible or changes size.
A scroll handler runs constantly and does layout checks on every scroll.
Observers let the browser do that work efficiently, which keeps scrolling smooth.
pushState changes the URL and adds a history entry without reloading the page.
When the user presses back or forward, a popstate event fires so the app can show the right view.
Frontend routers are built on these two pieces.
